j.learned_fact: Two different people's fingers leave different marks on a surface.
j.thinking_skill: comparing two observations and noticing they differ
j.notes: Two disconnected halves: the soccer arena opening goes nowhere, and the fingerprint idea is never made explicit enough for a 5-year-old to take away (why the marks differ is left unsaid).

j.learned_fact: Coin flips are independent: after four heads in a row the chance of tails on the next flip is still 50 percent (the gambler's fallacy).
j.thinking_skill: distinguishing independent events from perceived streaks, and separating fairness from kindness
j.notes: The laundry/skincare thread and the coin thread are joined only by the narrator asserting they feel like the same insight; 'reifying' in the mother's dialogue feels planted, though it is used correctly.

j.learned_fact: Practising a rhythm slowly first and then faster helps you learn it.
j.thinking_skill: imitating and repeating a pattern
j.notes: Almost no content beyond 'practice makes progress'; the First/Next/Then/Last scaffold reads as a checklist.

j.learned_fact: Sound waves from an approaching source are compressed (higher pitch) and from a receding source are stretched (lower pitch): the Doppler effect. Inaccuracies: the pitch does not keep climbing as a car approaches, it is steadily higher and then drops as it passes; the claim that this is 'the same principle' chemists use to study molecules is vague to the point of being misleading.
j.thinking_skill: connecting an experimental observation to an explanation and then transferring it to a new case (the recycling truck)
j.notes: The setup (dad driving in circles with the alarm on to test 'chemistry') is contrived, the physics is delivered as a bedtime explanation by mom, and 'vigorous spark' and 'sent him a signal' are forced vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: The three interior angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, so a missing angle can be found by subtracting the two known ones (60 + 70 = 130, so 50).
j.thinking_skill: deductive calculation of an unknown angle from a general rule
j.notes: The kite is treated as a triangle for the math but is called 'a small bright square' in the sky at the end; the repair (cut along the line, then tape a scrap into the gap) is muddled, and the right-angle/360 aside is recited rather than needed.

j.learned_fact: The pupil (the black dot in the middle of the eye) shrinks in bright light and grows larger in the dark.
j.thinking_skill: repeating a test (light on/off) to confirm a cause-and-effect observation
j.notes: The pupil discovery has nothing to do with the batting lesson beyond a pun on 'eyes wide open'; the 'had been ill' sentence and the ribbon prize are bolted on to tick vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: When a country's currency weakens, imports and foreign travel cost more in that currency while its exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, so exporters gain and importers lose.
j.thinking_skill: tracing one cause to opposite effects on two parties and weighing the trade-off
j.notes: Mom's explanation carries most of the concept and the 'thirty percent more than last month' figure is implausibly large for a currency move; 'apparatus of trade' is stiff. Grace's own verification (hotel prices) is a good touch.

j.learned_fact: Some pines have cones sealed shut with resin that only open and release their seeds when a wildfire's heat melts the seal, so seedlings carpet a burned forest the next year.
j.thinking_skill: inferring a mechanism by comparing two specimens with a before/after photo
j.notes: One garbled sentence ('didn't have seeds because the fire had destroyed them') contradicts the point it is making; otherwise a clean discovery story with the librarian only nudging.

j.learned_fact: The first mobile phone call was made in 1973 on a Motorola prototype weighing about 1.1 kg; a decade later the consumer version sold for nearly 4,000 dollars.
j.thinking_skill: historical empathy: reconstructing what a technology meant in its own era instead of judging it by today's standards
j.notes: 'Turgid with August heat' is a misuse (turgid means swollen or pompous, not sultry) and the 'cost less than a textbook' aside is clumsy; the classroom exercise itself is convincing and the facts check out.

j.learned_fact: Extreme results tend to be followed by more average ones (regression to the mean), so improvement after criticism or decline after praise is not evidence that the feedback caused it.
j.thinking_skill: conditional (if-then) reasoning to test and reject a causal hypothesis against a comparison case
j.notes: Dense for grade 9 and the closing 'stagnant water glass' line exists only to place a vocabulary word; 'Prieya' typo. The reasoning about Dewey and Marcus as disconfirming cases is genuinely good.

j.learned_fact: Round wheels roll smoothly; wheels with corners bump and stop.
j.thinking_skill: comparing two shapes' behaviour and generalising
j.notes: The cookie analogy is false: square cookies do not come out with 'bumpy, broken edges' because they have corners, so the lesson 'round is better' is taught through something untrue.

j.learned_fact: Touchscreens sense the electrical charge of a bare fingertip, not pressure, so ordinary gloves and pencil erasers do not register.
j.thinking_skill: recalling a principle and applying it to diagnose a failure after eliminating the pressure hypothesis
j.notes: Reads as middle-grade humour, younger than 13; it is never explained why Eli is wearing gloves indoors in the kitchen, which is the whole premise. Vocabulary (herbivore, robust, inherit) is used correctly.

j.learned_fact: A refrigerator moves heat out of its inside and releases it at the back, which is why the back feels warm.
j.thinking_skill: noticing a contrast (cold front, warm back) and asking why
j.notes: Raphael simply 'realized' the fridge pumps heat out with no reasoning or help, so the conclusion is unearned; 'That was the correct way it worked' is a planted vocabulary word, and the text is simpler than a 2nd-grade target.

j.learned_fact: A stick resting on a small rock works as a lever, and pushing farther from the pivot makes lifting a heavy load easier.
j.thinking_skill: testing cause and effect by changing hand position and comparing effort
j.notes: Hyperbole (a hippo-sized stone rolled by two small boys) stretches belief and the First/Next/Then/Last frame is used twice, but the humour and the drum rhythm keep it lively.

j.thinking_skill: proposing a fairness rule to resolve a group conflict
j.notes: 'Landmarks need both tall buildings and wide open spaces' is a nonsensical analogy built around a planted vocabulary word; the resolution (Coach 'listened' and everything was fixed by Thursday) is a bolted-on moral with no concrete mechanism.

j.learned_fact: Winds carry millions of tons of Saharan dust across the Atlantic every year, and the phosphorus in it fertilises the nutrient-poor soils of the Amazon.
j.thinking_skill: analogical reasoning between a cultural tradition and an ecological mechanism, plus probing a rule with a hypothetical
j.notes: Typo 'He did it as she showed her'; the dust/ofrenda rhyme is asserted a little too neatly, and Abuela's window speech lands the moral rather hard. The four-elements detail of the ofrenda is accurate.

j.learned_fact: Paying only the minimum on a credit-card balance takes years and costs hundreds in interest. But the story's facts are wrong: a 14-year-old cannot be issued a credit card even with cosigners; 60 dollars of interest on the first 1,200-dollar statement implies about 60 percent APR; and 25 dollars a month for five and a half years totals 1,650 dollars, i.e. 450 dollars of interest, not 'over six hundred'.
j.thinking_skill: computing the long-term cost of minimum payments
j.notes: The numbers do not add up and the premise is legally impossible; 'torrential list of charges' is a forced use of the vocabulary word. The final question to Marcus is a good beat.

j.learned_fact: A taped square of straws squashes into a diamond when pushed, but a triangle keeps its shape, so triangles make a strong tower.
j.thinking_skill: comparing two shapes under a push and choosing the stronger one to build with
j.notes: Sound and age-appropriate, but the First/Next/Then/Last sequencing is mechanical and stacking four triangles does not really make a 'tall' tower.

j.learned_fact: In genuine financial records the leading digit 1 appears about a third of the time while 7s and 9s are rare (Benford's law); leading digits spread evenly across 1-9 are a sign the numbers were fabricated.
j.thinking_skill: inferring fabrication from a digit distribution while separating what the evidence proves (alteration) from what it cannot (motive)
j.notes: The uncle hands his own doctored books to a teenager to check and then confesses in two lines; 'a pattern that seemed to obfuscate rather than clarify' misuses obfuscate (the pattern is what clarifies). A 17-year-old working on 'the playroom floor' is an odd choice.

j.learned_fact: Teenagers' body clocks shift later than young children's, so they naturally get sleepy around 10:30-11 pm, which is why an early first bell suits small children better than teens.
j.thinking_skill: gathering data to test a hypothesis and recognising that a one-person sample is not enough
j.notes: 'She recounted' is a misuse (recount means to narrate past events, not read out a draft); the eventual five data points are still tiny, though the story is honest about needing more.

j.learned_fact: A square frame squashes into a diamond but a triangle holds its shape, so triangles make a sturdy roof.
j.thinking_skill: trial-and-error comparison leading to a general rule
j.notes: 'Mattress', 'ill' and 'quiet room' are slightly planted, but the warm framing (cookies for a sick mom) carries the structural lesson naturally.

j.learned_fact: A growling tummy is the stomach squeezing and moving air around, and it means you are hungry.
j.thinking_skill: connecting a body signal to a need
j.notes: The mechanism sentence is dropped in by the narrator rather than discovered, and the closing 'tell a grown-up nearby' safety message is bolted on.

j.learned_fact: Children need nine to twelve hours of sleep a night, and the hormone that makes you grow is mostly released while you sleep.
j.thinking_skill: linking lack of sleep to poor performance and building a routine to fix it
j.notes: The facts arrive as a three-sentence lecture from mom; 'ran past him like a purr of wind' misuses 'purr'; the First/Next/Then/Last rule and the instant win are formulaic.

j.learned_fact: An overall acceptance rate can favour one group even when every individual department favours the other, if the groups apply in different proportions to departments with different acceptance rates (Simpson's paradox).
j.thinking_skill: disaggregating data to test whether an aggregate statistic supports a causal claim, and recognising what the evidence still cannot settle
j.notes: Name inconsistency (Mr. Aldous / Mr. Aldoss) and 49 applicants is a thin sample for four studios; otherwise the zine-craft frame and the statistics interlock convincingly and the vocabulary (extol, pragmatism, conciliatory, colophon) is used correctly.

j.learned_fact: Radiocarbon dating works on once-living material, the half-life of carbon-14 is about 5,700 years, and the method reaches back about 50,000 years. But the story's conclusion is false: wood dated to 1962 does not contradict a guitar being bought in 1969 (wood is cut and seasoned before an instrument is built), and the claim that the half-life makes recent decades 'pretty precise' is wrong (any precision for 1960s wood comes from bomb-pulse calibration, not the half-life).
j.thinking_skill: weighing family legend against physical evidence (but drawing an invalid inference from it)
j.notes: The central inference is broken: the lab result the story treats as debunking the legend is fully consistent with it. 'He acquiesce to the idea' is ungrammatical, and Marcus delivers the carbon-dating facts as a mini-lecture.

j.learned_fact: A properly random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly plus or minus 3 points regardless of population size; how randomly the sample is drawn matters more than how large the population is.
j.thinking_skill: identifying sampling bias and redesigning a survey to correct it
j.notes: The characters are explicitly eighth graders for a 9th-grade target; the key concept is read straight off a website as a definition, and surveying 847 students in two weeks with eight kids strains belief. The arithmetic (41/52 is about 79 percent) is right.

j.learned_fact: Radiocarbon dating works on once-living material such as wood, bone or cloth, with a carbon-14 half-life of about 5,730 years, and is useful back to roughly 50,000 years. The story does not notice that an 800-year date is the age of the wood, not the instrument (no guitar is 800 years old), so 'bought an antique' does not follow.
j.thinking_skill: weighing two competing explanations and spotting a hidden assumption
j.notes: Good voice and a real 'hidden assumption' move, but the story conflates the wood's age with the guitar's age throughout ('the eight-hundred-year-old wood', 'bought an antique'), which is the very kind of unexamined assumption it claims to expose.

j.learned_fact: A sound source moving toward you sounds higher-pitched and one moving away sounds lower (Doppler effect), so pitch rather than loudness tells you the direction.
j.thinking_skill: redesigning a test by isolating the relevant variable (pitch instead of loudness)
j.notes: Typo 'Mayay'; 'a vigorous thumbs-up' is planted vocabulary; the closing salt-water idea is a weak test for atoms, and one line again has the pitch 'climbing up and up' as the car approaches, which is not how the Doppler shift sounds.

j.learned_fact: The brain uses about 20 percent of the body's energy while being only about 2 percent of its weight. The story's leap that a hard test made his brain burn far more fuel is not supported (mental effort barely changes the brain's energy use), and 'as much energy as arms, legs and stomach combined' is invented.
j.thinking_skill: using a read fact to explain a personal observation
j.notes: The true fact is stretched into a popular myth (thinking hard makes you hungry); 'arrange the facts' is forced vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: Light bends where it leaves the water, so a fish looks shallower than it really is; to catch it you aim below where it appears.
j.thinking_skill: inferring an invisible cause from a repeated failure and testing a corrected strategy
j.notes: Maya is 'on dinner strike' and then takes Declan off her 'boycott list', a loose use of boycott; the citation/corrosive care-sheet opening is a slightly artificial way to seat two vocabulary words.

j.thinking_skill: asking for help politely when a goal is out of reach
j.notes: A manners lesson with no factual content; the helper praising 'good asking for help' makes the moral explicit, and 'some were messy and mixed up' is a stray detail.

j.learned_fact: Price depends on scarcity relative to demand, not on usefulness: water is cheap because it is plentiful even though one bottle is worth everything to someone dying of thirst, while diamonds are dear because few exist and many want them (the diamond-water paradox).
j.thinking_skill: reconciling two apparently contradictory observations through marginal reasoning
j.notes: The concept is delivered in a long explanatory speech from Marcus, and 'Devon sounded impetuous' is a slightly off use of the word; the hiker and Mrs. Chen vignettes are good evidence-gathering.

j.learned_fact: The back of a refrigerator feels warm even though the inside is cold.
j.thinking_skill: noticing an anomaly and asking why
j.notes: The helmet build and the warm fridge are two unrelated episodes stapled together, the question is raised and abandoned, and a cat sleeping behind a fridge is a stretch; text is simpler than a 2nd-grade target.

j.learned_fact: Tim Berners-Lee created the first web page at CERN in 1991, and in 1993 CERN released the web's underlying technology royalty-free so anyone could use it.
j.thinking_skill: counterfactual reasoning about how a licensing decision shaped everything that followed
j.notes: Vocabulary misuse: 'the mendacity of her own earlier assumption' (mendacity means lying, not error) and 'the incipient world that would have existed'; 'had enthrall her' is ungrammatical. A local HTML page in a workshop is not 'live on the internet', and the reflective passages repeat the same point three times.

j.learned_fact: An airbag inflates within tens of milliseconds, faster than a blink, and then immediately deflates through vents to cushion the impact, so it is already going flat by the time a person notices it.
j.thinking_skill: revising a model to match a real-world observation
j.notes: Flat and simplistic for a 15-year-old; the coding assignment (an animation that materialises from a few lines) is hand-waved, and 'missing something irrelevant to the basic mechanics or actually important' is a clumsy sentence built to place a vocabulary word.

j.learned_fact: Benford's law (about 30 percent of leading digits are 1, under 5 percent are 9) only detects fabricated numbers when the data vary naturally; fixed prices like a 9-dollar ticket break that assumption, so the test says nothing about honesty.
j.thinking_skill: checking whether a statistical test's assumptions hold before acting on its result
j.notes: A 19-dollar entry is found in the 'mountain of nines' pile though it starts with 1; the four-hundred-dollar discrepancy is left open (deliberately). Vocabulary (impetuous, obfuscate, fortitude) is used correctly.

j.learned_fact: A lighthouse's light shows boats where the rocks are so they steer away from them, not toward them.
j.thinking_skill: correcting another child's misconception with an explanation
j.notes: The knocked-over toy pile is filler and the shop scene is generic, but the lighthouse exchange is a genuine small idea told through play.

j.learned_fact: With a pulley, pulling down on one end of the rope makes the load on the other end go up.
j.thinking_skill: replicating a demonstrated mechanism on his own
j.notes: Dylan's own build has a rope and a flag but no wheel, so it is not a pulley; 'took a calm breath' is planted and the prose is flat.

j.learned_fact: Doubling an object's length multiplies its surface area and cross-section by 4 but its volume and weight by 8 (square-cube law), which is why giant insects cannot exist and elephants need thick legs.
j.thinking_skill: quantitative proportional reasoning plus recognising the limits of what the model can decide
j.notes: Minor typo ('two in night in February'); the 1.5x figures (about 3.4 and about 2.25) are correct and the 'math is a floor, not a map' reflection is earned rather than tacked on.

j.learned_fact: Follower counts say little about how many people someone actually has two-way conversations with.
j.thinking_skill: reframing a failed hypothesis into a measurable question about the gap itself
j.notes: 'Historicize her approach' is a misuse (historicize does not mean break into steps) and 'a sullen quality' is odd; scraping classmates' messages at midnight passes without comment, and no verifiable fact is offered, only the story's own invented numbers.

j.learned_fact: A car's airbag is triggered by a deceleration sensor, inflates in about 30 milliseconds via a chemical charge that produces nitrogen gas, then deflates through vents, so it is already flat before you finish blinking.
j.thinking_skill: changing one variable at a time to isolate a bug
j.notes: The debugging logic is inconsistent: the comparison is described as greater-than at the start, he flips it to less-than, then flips it 'back to greater-than' and the same code now behaves differently. The voice and the uncle scene are excellent.

j.learned_fact: Touchscreens respond to bare fingertips but not to ordinary gloves.
j.thinking_skill: a controlled on/off experiment to isolate the cause
j.notes: Eli never learns why gloves fail (no mention of conductivity or capacitance), so the takeaway is only the symptom; 'become a herbivore and only respond to plants' misuses the vocabulary word as a non-joke, and 'robust in her opinions' is strained. The final text to Marcus ('why does your phone work with gloves') contradicts everything before it.
